newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea accuses North of manipulating food data.
newsitem.headline: South Korea accuses North of manipulating food data.

text.p: A senior South Korean official on Wednesday accused North Korea of manipulating data to exaggerate hunger and depravation in the country in a bid to secure more international food aid.

Vice National Unification Minister Kim Suk-woo told a seminar on North Korea that the Seoul government would not rush to help North Korea until Pyongyang takes steps to end its chronic problem of food shortages.
"North Korea releases statistics as it wishes. The North is a country where a lot of things are stage- managed to serve its purposes," he said.
"On February 3, North Korea announced it only had 240,000 tonnes of food left. If it told the truth, food must have run out by the end of February," he said.
Kim said there was no doubt the Stalinist country was suffering from an acute food shortage, but that warnings by international aid groups that Pyongyang faced imminent famine were exaggerated.
He said the aid groups' assessments of the North Korean food situation were based on statistics and explanations provided by Pyongyang.
Kim said the nation spent about $900 million annually for political propaganda and set aside one quarter of its state budget on defence, despite its appeals for food to avert famine.
"If North Korea reduces its defence spendings by five percent, it could buy about two million tonnes of corn and meet its food needs," he added.
Seoul has made clear large-scale assistance was unlikely unless Pyongyang began dismantling its military machine and showed it was ready to repay food with goodwill peace gestures.

The United States and South Korea are seeking to convince North Korea to join four-nation talks aimed at securing a peace treaty to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War. The talks also involve China.

North Korea in April agreed to join the four-nation talks if it was first guaranteed large-scale food aid and an easing of U.S. trade sanctions. Washington and Seoul say such aid could be discussed during the talks.
Last week, U.N. officials said North Korea was on the brink of a major humanitarian crisis and needed outside help within weeks.

Peter McDermott, deputy director of emergency programmes at the United Nations Children's Fund, said Pyongyang would have to stop a paltry daily ration of 100 grammes (3.5 oz) of rice to its citizens on June 20 as food supplies and fuel dry up.
